prize_parts.citation: for unifying electronic-structure theory and molecular dynamics, enabling first-principles simulation of the dynamics of molecules and materials

statement.case_for: I keep Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B016) as my preferred single part. The 1985 invention let nuclei move on electronic ground-state surfaces computed on the fly, and it created ab initio dynamics of liquids, solids, interfaces and reactive chemistry, a capability that had no predecessor. It rests on one paper and two names, so the committee can award it without trimming any credit. Four decades of independent use, implementation in many codes and routine application to bond breaking, proton transfer in water and surface catalysis make it fully mature. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened this case: the whole discussion of the leading candidate has been about who must be left out and what has not yet been approved, and B016 faces neither question.
statement.case_against: The practical weakness is breadth of support. Only Linke and Brzezinski rank it among their alternatives, and no one else prefers it, so a vote for it may simply split the field. The 1998 DFT prize and the 2013 multiscale prize mean a third computational award is a real objection, and a methods prize may read as further from experimental chemistry than degraders or C-N coupling. A citation anchored on the 1985 paper also leaves Parrinello's later work (metadynamics, machine-learned potentials) outside the prize. I have not found a way to answer the 'already served' objection other than by saying that ab initio dynamics is a different capability from DFT energies or QM/MM, and I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof. If the committee judges that argument insufficient, my vote goes to B005 for maturity and attribution, and to B037 only if the credit and approval questions are resolved.

responses.point: Sparr now prefers B037 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, treats the cereblon glue mechanism as a separate and decisive discovery, and says B016 is cleaner on attribution but computational chemistry has been recognised recently and could wait for a later year.
responses.response: Her own words in round 1 concede the two points I care about: B016 is cleaner on attribution, and the glue branch is a distinct discovery. If the glue mechanism is decisive and separate from the PROTAC concept, then the single trio she supports is exactly the construction she says may be better recognised as two achievements. That is a credit problem, not a detail. I do not agree that recent recognition of computation argues for waiting. 1998 honoured density functional theory and 2013 honoured multiscale QM/MM modelling, neither of which provides first-principles dynamics. I take her point that a drug-modality prize is a weaker fit for Chemistry than a method, though in her framing that favours B005 or B016 over B037. I have not changed my view on this.

responses.point: Somfai argues that the Nobel criterion is the chemical discovery and its reproducibility, not an approved drug, and says B016 will be harder to defend for its chemical consequences than a new modality.
responses.response: I accept his criterion about discovery over approval and I agree that PROTAC reproducibility is not in doubt. But the same criterion helps B016: the consequences are documented in the chemistry of water, ionic solutions, defects, catalysis at surfaces and reaction mechanisms studied with first-principles dynamics, and these are chemical questions. Where I differ is on attribution, which his own AGAINST section calls real. Applying the criterion he states, a prize is easier to defend when it does not require leaving out Sakamoto, Ciulli, Gray, Ito and Kim. He names B005 as the safer choice if B037 is early, and on that fallback we agree.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, prefers B037 but ranks B016 second and says that timeliness of impact on drug discovery and biology should come ahead of overdueness alone, while admitting his first place may reflect an appealing story more than a settled verdict.
responses.response: His admission that first place may reflect narrative appeal is the most useful sentence in the B037 case, and I take it seriously. I agree that overdueness is not by itself a reason to award a prize. My argument is instead that B016 combines three properties that B037 lacks at the moment: a bounded invention, two names that nobody disputes, and settled impact. Linke asks whether a pure methods prize is the best use of this year. I would answer that the committee has the choice between a method that is complete and a concept whose credit and clinical record are still moving. I stay where I was, but I recognise he and I are closer than the headline preferences suggest.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers B005 as a stable, well-attributed prize but notes the overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize and the Kosugi and Migita question, and holds B016 as a comparable alternative.
responses.response: We agree that B005 and B016 are the two most mature and best attributed options. I would only add that the overlap with 2010 is a larger problem for B005 than the overlap with 1998 and 2013 is for B016, because B005 is the same catalyst logic applied to a different bond, while Car-Parrinello opened a different capability. In round 1 I said I would not fight a Buchwald-Hartwig prize, and that remains true. If the committee cannot unite behind my first choice, B005 is where my vote would go, ahead of B037.

responses.point: Chabes moved from base editing to B037 because it was ranked by all eight members, and says he is less able to judge B016 and would defer to colleagues in computational and physical chemistry.
responses.response: I understand deferring on a field outside one's own, and I note that my own subject-closeness to simulation is the reason I have stated a conflict note. On breadth of support, I would separate counting from scientific merit: appearing on all eight ballots tells us B037 is a safe name for a ranking, but it does not settle the three-name cut that he himself lists as his first uncertainty. His question of whether PROTACs and glues are one idea or two is one I cannot answer from his citation, which joins them. His point about an unnatural split of three names is fair, and it is the reason I am not now proposing B016 with a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a third computational-chemistry prize (after 1998 and 2013) as acceptable given that B016 supplies first-principles dynamics, which neither earlier prize did.
Whether a B016 citation should stay tied to the 1985 invention or mention Parrinello's later methods. I would leave them out so that the award stays with the unified method.
Whether a first regulatory approval of a PROTAC, or a settled three-name credit for B037, would change my fallback from B005 to B037.
I have not independently checked usage or citation figures for any candidate and rely on the shortlist and the round 1 statements.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My postdoctoral EVB collaboration was with Arieh Warshel, who is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. I work in the same broad area of biomolecular simulation as B016 and have used related methods, which I state as subject-closeness and not as a personal or institutional tie to Roberto Car or Michele Parrinello. No recusal is warranted, and none has been proposed by others.
